articles.headline: The one thing everyone can do to fight for free and fair elections
keyFacts: Brennan Center deputy director Eliza Sweren-Becker told Vox that voting is the key way to counter campaigns undermining trust in democracy.
Sweren-Becker stated that final election results may take days because states must count every properly cast ballot.
Sweren-Becker said Congress has the constitutional power to enact national voting access rules and restore the Voting Rights Act.
body: ﻿It’s an anxious moment for American voters: Will we have a free and fair election — or not? | Spencer Platt/Getty Images

Election Day is almost here — but even after the first Tuesday after the first Monday in November, the election won’t really be over. The vote count will take days or even weeks in some states. President Donald Trump seems certain to raise objections to results he doesn’t like — he’s already getting started in Alaska — and he has threatened to marshal the forces of the federal government in his efforts.

It’s an anxious moment for American voters: Will we have a free and fair election — or not? Luckily, says Eliza Sweren-Becker, deputy director in the Brennan Center’s Voting Rights and Elections Program, there is still one thing that every American 18 and older can do to make sure their voice is heard: vote.

“I think that is the intent. It’s to create a lack of confidence. It’s to discourage voters from participating,” Sweren-Becker told Vox’s Astead Herndon on America, Actually . “But the only way that that campaign to undermine our confidence and to sow distrust actually works is if voters stay home. The way to defeat that attempt to shake voters’ trust in democracy is just to participate.”

Sweren-Becker spoke with Astead about what states could do to speed up their vote counts and ensure everyone has a chance to cast their ballot, the need to restore the Voting Rights Act, and the long-term impact of Trump’s election denialism.

Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full show, so listen to America, Actually wherever you get your podcasts or watch it on Vox’s YouTube channel .

Let’s start with Election Day. More than a dozen states count late-arriving ballots. President Donald Trump has used the shifting vote counts as pretense to further his own election interference claims.
How prepared should folks be for a long wait in November for results? And how that could impact confidence in the results?
You’re absolutely right that we may get results out of states or in certain races in the days following Election Day. Voters should not expect to have the final result on Election Day.
And when you hear reporting on the news that somebody’s ahead or somebody’s behind, remember: They haven’t counted all the votes yet.
The critical thing is we need to count every vote, and every person’s vote needs to be counted.

So while it is true that some states allow ballots to arrive after Election Day, they all have to be cast by Election Day. The Supreme Court just this year said that it’s totally appropriate for states to set their own ballot receipt deadlines. We have to be patient, as an American electorate, to get the proper results to count every ballot and make sure all the voices are heard.

But isn’t it kinda wild that we can’t get results on election night? I saw Donald Trump cite the Brazilian presidential election, and while I know he’s doing that from a self-interested place, I did think for a second: Why does it take so long for us to put these results together?

I could totally understand why people would prefer the results faster. And candidly, could states do better at preparing and counting faster? Sure. But they have limited resources. They are working their butts off to prepare for the election with the staff that they have, and then they work tremendously hard to count properly, accurately, as fast as they can.

Could states change their policies to allow them, in some places, to pre-process ballots, to allow them to get to results faster? Sure. I’m not saying states shouldn’t change their policies to create more efficiency here. But given the rules of the road that we have, we need to make sure that every properly cast ballot is counted.
If I’m someone who is concerned about election security and free and fair elections, what should I be looking out for?
So, for example, I have heard that there is some anxiety about mail voting.

If you want to cast a mail ballot, just know that you probably have a bunch of options in your state as to how you can cast it. You can certainly rely on the mail and have USPS deliver that ballot, but of course, we know occasionally mail gets delayed. Your state may have ballot drop boxes. You may have ballot drop-off at election officials’ offices, or even at polling places.
Find out your options.

Yes, definitely find out your options. Voters should also check their voter registration status. Make sure it’s up to date with their current address. Of course, if you’re not registered to vote and you still have time in your state to register, please do register.

Everyone should participate. Our democracy works best the more of us that can participate. If your registration date has not passed, don’t forget to register to vote. Vote with your friends, vote with your community, vote with your family. Voting should be joyful. It’s a civic experience that I think is really fun.
I try to take my kids with me to vote because it’s exciting. They get stickers. Everyone loves stickers .
It’s half the reason I go.
It’s also a reminder. You get your sticker, other people see you, they know it’s Election Day, maybe they go out to vote.
It’s a way to be part of your community and invest in your community and to choose who you want to be a leader of your community.
What about after Election Day?

Earlier this year, Democrats and Republicans in Congress circulated a letter asking members to commit to recognizing state-certified winners and “oppose any attempt to refuse or delay a seating of a member-elect.” We saw House Speaker Mike Johnson delay the swearing-in of an Arizona representative last year,
That seems to me like maybe a preview of what might be to come. How fearful should we be of these post-election attempts to block members from being seated?

I think those scenarios are highly unlikely. I understand why folks are worried about them, but the reality is, states have their own certification processes, which are laid out in state law and that are mandatory for them to follow. It is not discretionary whether states certify their elections. So once there is a new Congress, we have confidence that they will be seated according to how the voters actually cast their ballots.

I want to end by thinking about Trump’s consistent questioning of the integrity of our election system. If he ultimately doesn’t try to actually steal the election, what is the long-term impact of his relentless focus on it and support for policies like the Save America Act?

Just because we have won in many courts against this administration doesn’t delude me into thinking that this administration is just going to stop in this years-long campaign to sow doubt in our election systems.

I think that is the intent. It’s to create a lack of confidence. It’s to discourage voters from participating. And to some degree, I think the administration has succeeded in creating some confusion about the rules or a lack of confidence. But the only way that that campaign to undermine our confidence and to sow distrust actually works is if voters stay home.

The way to defeat that attempt to shake voters’ trust in democracy is to participate in our democracy and to turn out and to make their voices heard regardless of party, regardless of candidate. To say that we will not be made to fear participation in our democracy, but we are going to continue to seize it and take joy in it and show that we deserve a stronger representative democracy that serves all Americans.
What are things that could happen to inspire trust in our electoral system? Are there reforms that you think might make the public feel a reinvigorated sense of confidence?

There are certainly things that Congress could do to create a national floor of voter access and ensure that someone’s right to vote doesn’t depend on what state they live in. That includes basic reforms like same-day registration, online voter registration, universal access to mail voting that doesn’t require strict satisfaction of certain excuse requirements, which still exists in many states.

I think it’s time for Congress to ban partisan gerrymandering. I also think it’s time to restore the Voting Rights Act, and Congress can enact a statutory right to vote that is meaningfully enforceable so that voters can go to court if their voting rights have been burdened, and they can get a real remedy.

That has been really undermined by the Supreme Court, but Congress can and should respond. They have it within their power. The Constitution gives Congress the power to set rules for elections. They should.

articles.headline: Epstein files take back seat in midterms but experts say issue has not gone away
keyFacts: Survivors' advocates expressed concern that the Jeffrey Epstein scandal is receding during US midterms, though experts say the issue remains.
Advocates and lawmakers are demanding the release of full Epstein files, while voters balance the scandal with immediate daily financial concerns.
Experts expect Congress to revisit the Epstein investigation and transparency legislation after midterms, especially if Democrats win control of a chamber.
body: As US voters head to the polls for crucial and fraught midterm elections, some survivors’ advocates in the Jeffrey Epstein investigation have expressed concern that the scandal could recede into the background.

Political experts believe, however, the Epstein issue is not going away permanently and that many voters can balance day-to-day concerns such as affordability and AI with the scandal involving the late financier and accused sex trafficker whose social circle was widespread among America’s elite.

“My greatest concern is not that the public will forget Jeffrey Epstein, but that the politicians and institutions responsible for accountability will use the chaos of world events as an excuse to move on,” said Spencer Kuvin of Goldlaw, who has represented multiple Epstein survivors.

Kuvin added: “Wars, economic crises and political controversies may dominate the headlines, but they do not erase the suffering of the victims or the unanswered questions about how Epstein and his powerful associates were allowed to operate for decades.

“Justice should not have an expiration date, and it certainly should not be dictated by the news cycle. We cannot allow the Epstein scandal to become yesterday’s news simply because today’s headlines are more urgent.”
Kuvin called for the US government to continue releasing Epstein files – which many have said were excluded from allegedly incomplete disclosures – and for Congress to demand accountability.

“It has been disappointing to have seen attention diverted from Jeffrey Epstein in the past year,” said Jennifer Freeman of Marsh Law, who represents numerous Epstein survivors in litigation surrounding his sexual abuse of teenage girls.

Freeman, however, expressed optimism about the long-term prospects of justice for survivors, saying: “While public attention may have shifted from the Epstein case, given the electoral cycle, I am confident it will command concentration and accountability shortly again.”

Freeman noted that she was continuing to pursue a lawsuit against the US government for alleged negligence “in repeatedly, for decades, dropping the ball on investigating and prosecuting Epstein”. She is also litigating a class-action lawsuit against his estate related to his collection and production of child sex abuse images.
Political experts said that Epstein might get less attention from campaigning politicians and voters, but that it was probably a temporary dip, not a permanent drop-off.

“It really does feel like everything is on fire. I think people can care about several things at once, but what’s directly affecting their lives tends to take priority,” Brittany Martinez, a Republican strategist who works as acting director of Principles First, said. “When they’re worried about gas prices, living costs and whether their government is working for them, that can push Epstein out of the immediate conversation.

“I don’t think the questions or the demand for answers have gone away; they’re just competing for attention. So I’d expect to hear less about it for stretches, rather than see it disappear altogether.”
“There’s just something every day with Trump,” said Shawn Donahue, clinical associate professor in the University at Buffalo’s department of political science.

For Donahue, timing also plays a key role. The US Congress has been in recess and without members on the House floor, so there’s not any discussion of the Epstein Files Transparency Act’s proposed new iteration. This bill, the Epstein Files Transparency Act II, seeks to address what advocates have said are shortfalls in the present EFTA – such as an absence of enforcement mechanisms.

“It kind of feels like whenever Congress comes back into session, this probably starts to become more of an issue again, and especially if Democrats are looking at being in control of one or maybe both chambers of Congress,” Donahue said.
Should Democrats win the house, as polls project, Donahue expects they will swiftly “put Republicans on the spot” with Epstein. “Democrats are ready to start on the investigation from day one.”

For Julie Roginsky, who co-founded the non-profit Lift Our Voices and pursued a sexual harassment lawsuit against the former Fox News CEO Roger Ailes, the significance of Epstein among voters has not gone away.

“I think Epstein is part of the reason that Trump’s numbers are at record lows. I think it’s something that was one of the issues where even Maga Republicans broke with him,” Roginsky said. “I think that if Democrats do get control of at least one house of Congress this year, then starting next year, you’re going to see a lot more conversation about survivors and about Epstein.”
Congressional supporters of survivors said they would keep fighting for truth and justice.

“This is bigger than a moment. It’s a reckoning, and Americans are ready to have this conversation about power, abuse, and who gets protected,” the Democratic New Mexico representative Teresa Leger Fernández said in a statement. “Of course, Americans will vote with their pocketbooks. They’re worried about groceries, gas, and making rent. But they won’t forget that this president was Epstein’s friend and tried to hide the truth from them.

“The survivors have fought for decades to be heard. Our responsibility is to keep fighting alongside them, get the truth out, and hold those responsible accountable. That responsibility doesn’t disappear when the headlines change.”

The Massachusetts Democratic representative Ayanna Pressley said in a statement: “Justice for survivors of Epstein’s abuse has been a prominent issue amongst the electorate because people of conscience see through the cover-ups of the Trump Administration and demand accountability – that won’t change no matter how much they try to flood the zone and distract us.”
Pressley and fellow representatives Leger Fernández and Deborah Ross recently introduced legislation to address survivors’ financial burdens.

The New Mexico Democratic senator Ben Ray Luján similarly commented that whatever might be unfolding, he would keep pushing for the files to be released in full despite the Department of Justice insisting they have released all Epstein investigative files required under the law.
“We cannot lose sight of the need to release the full Epstein files, hold those responsible accountable, and ensure survivors receive the justice they deserve,” Luján said.
Asked for comment, the White House insisted Trump had advocated for survivors.

“Just as President Trump has said, he’s been totally exonerated on anything relating to Epstein. And by releasing thousands of pages of documents, cooperating with the House Oversight Committee’s subpoena request, signing the Epstein Files Transparency Act, and calling for more investigations into Epstein’s Democrat friends, President Trump has done more for Epstein’s victims than anyone before him,” the White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said in a statement.
The statement then claimed that several Democrats had yet to explain why they were soliciting money and meetings from Epstein after he was a convicted sex offender.

As for the Department of Justice, the department maintains they have complied with disclosure requirements under the original EFTA. They also rejected claims by New Mexico’s attorney general, Raúl Torrez, that the justice department had not been helping the state’s investigation.

“The Epstein Files Transparency Act does not require, and the protective orders in place in the Southern District of New York do not permit, disclosure of victim-identifying information carte blanche, and New Mexico has provided no lawful basis to justify such sweeping disclosures,” the department said in a statement. “Protecting victim privacy remains a top priority for the Department, and neither [legal] requests nor a desire to cooperate outweighs that privacy. DOJ remains available to assist New Mexico’s investigation consistent with the law and binding court orders.”

articles.headline: 5 Years Later, Metroid Dread’s Perfect Ending Is Still One of Nintendo’s Best
keyFacts: Polygon published an article examining the enduring impact of the 2021 video game Metroid Dread and its defining ending.
The article explains that protagonist Samus Aran struggles throughout the game as Metroid DNA progressively takes over her body.
The author notes that developer MercurySteam will continue these narrative themes in the upcoming follow-up game, Metroid Ravenous.
body: Five years after its release, Metroid Dread still occupies a permanent space in my brain. Samus Aran’s nightmarish escape from a robot-infested abyss successfully revitalized the dormant Metroid series in 2021 by delivering a tightly designed Metroidvania full of challenging battles. There’s so much that’s still vivid in my memory now, but there’s one moment I have come back to time and time again: that ending.
[Ed. note: This article contains spoilers for Metroid Dread.]

Metroid Dread begins when the Galactic Federation dispatches Samus to Planet ZDR. The mission is to recover the Federation’s lost EMMI robots, who were sent to the planet to find the last living X parasites hiding in the universe. Samus has a vested interest in that mission considering that those are the parasites that nearly killed her in Metroid Fusion, and now threaten to become an invasive species if left unchecked. The simple retrieval operation goes south in a hurry when a Chozo warrior named Raven Beak attacks and leaves her stranded deep underground — without her power-ups, of course.

That kicks off a horror-tinged escape story where a powerless Samus becomes prey to the reprogrammed EMMI Why do the robots want her dead? To extract the Metroid DNA swirling around in Samus’ blood following the events of Fusion. Samus was fused with the DNA at the start of that game to save her life after an X parasite attack, but it turns out that the risky operation painted a target on her back in the long-run.

While there are multiple story threads at play in Dread, Samus’ relationship to her own body is the real heart of the story. Underneath all the Chozo lore is a personal horror story about a woman slowly becoming the very thing that she dedicated her life to killing.

Samus has always had a complicated relationship to the energy-sucking Metroid species. In the series’ first game, they are played as straight baddies. They’re evil monsters that you need to shoot. Metroid 2: Return of Samus seems like it’s doubling down on that for the bulk of the adventure until the very end. After eradicating the universe’s last living Metroid, a baby hatches and imprints onto Samus. The game ends with an eerily silent trek back up to the surface with your new pal, letting you sit with the extinction you’ve just carried out without question. Super Metroid twists the knife even further when that bay Metroid sacrifices its life to save Samus. Samus is not the hero in the first few Metroid games; she is a weapon.

That makes her struggles with the DNA overtaking her body all the more powerful in Dread. In the game’s finest moment, Samus is jumped by an enemy and instinctively rears her arm back to suck the energy out of it, like a Metroid would. She catches herself at the last second and instead blasts it with the canon on her other arm. There’s a look of terror on her face as she realizes that she nearly lost control of her body to her Metroid brain. The entire dynamic is captured in her two arms, which come to represent the war inside of her.

That battle comes to a head in Dread’s unnerving ending. As she finds herself on the brink of death in a climactic battle against Raven Beak, Samus finally loses full control of her body. The Metroid DNA fully takes over in a Kafkaesque metamorphosis that leaves her in a monstrous green suit. How DNA transforms a metal space suit is beyond me, but it’s an effective metaphor nonetheless.

I imagine that the sequence was designed to be badass, with Samus unleashing her ultimate power to defeat Raven Beak, but it still haunts me to this day. It’s a terrifying moment that brings Samus' deepest held fear to fruition. She quite literally becomes a Metroid, the very thing she drove to extinction. Is she even in control of her body during the fight, or is she acting on animal instinct? The more you put it in context of a story about your past consuming you, the more the Metroid suit feels like a curse rather than a superpower. Even when Samus returns back to normal at the end of the game, she flies off into space as a hunted woman.

It’s part of the reason that I’m so eager to see where next year’s follow-up, Metroid Ravenous, takes the saga next. Its first trailer indicates that developer MercurySteam is leaning into Dread’s themes even more, as Samus has now been reduced to a pure animal state. Again, her arm tells the story: her instinct to use her arm to suck the life out of enemies has won. It’s a full-blown game mechanic now that’s imperative to her survival. We even get a few glimpses at the Metroid Suit, which looks like it will play a bigger role in the game.

Is it a distressing sign that the Samus we know is gone? Or has she embraced the power of a species that was unjustly massacred by humans? If handled delicately, Ravenous stands to add an exciting wrinkle to Samus’ long, complicated relationship to Metroidkind.

articles.headline: Gunmen open fire at a church during a funeral in Jordan, killing 7 and wounding 40
keyFacts: Authorities said gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church in Jordan on Friday, killing seven people and wounding 40 others.
A government statement said the attack was carried out by unknown assailants and investigations are underway at full speed.
Jordan declared three days of national mourning, and King Abdullah II stated that the country will confront the terrorist act with the harshest penalties.
body: Gunmen open fire at a church during a funeral in Jordan, killing 7 and wounding 40
JERUSALEM — Gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a church in Jordan on Friday, killing seven people and wounding 40 others, authorities said.
The shooting took place at a Greek Orthodox church in Karak, about 90 kilometers (55 miles) south of the capital, Amman.

Footage broadcast on Jordanian state television showed two gunmen who appear to be holding pistols approaching the church and firing shots. A third man who appears to be holding a semiautomatic rifle then approaches and opens fire, and all three then run toward the church.
Video footage taken by witnesses shows broken glass and pools of blood on the floor of the church.

Dorgham Halasa, who was among the mourners inside the church, said intense gunfire erupted 15 minutes after the funeral had started, and then people started running. "It was a weird situation, and heavy gunfire," Halasa said.

He did not see the gunmen, but said other people reported seeing four of them. The Associated Press could not independently verify the number of assailants, and Jordan's security services did not immediately release details.

A government statement said that the attack was "carried out by unknown assailants," but didn't say whether any gunmen were captured or killed. It said that "investigations are underway at full speed."
Jordan declared three days of national mourning, according to the kingdom's Petra News Agency.
Karak is home to a minority Christian population.

In 2016, gunmen ambushed police in a series of attacks in Karak, including at a Crusader castle popular with tourists, killing 10 people, including seven officers, and wounding dozens. Jordanian security forces killed those gunmen after a long standoff.
Jordan's Health Minister Ibrahim al-Budour said two of those wounded are in critical condition.

King Abdullah II said on X that Jordan "will confront the terrorist act that targeted Karak with the harshest penalties" and offered his "deepest condolences to the families of the martyrs, and our wishes for recovery to the wounded."

Jordan's Prime Minister Jafar Hassan said during a security meeting in Karak on Friday evening that the attack was a result of terrorist ideology and blind extremism. He said the assailants will be punished and legal measures taken against those who seek to introduce extremism.
Condemnation of the slayings came from around the region, including from Lebanon, Syria, Egypt and Oman.

Ahmed al-Tayeb in Cairo, the grand imam of Al-Azhar, the Sunni Muslim world's foremost religious institution, offered his condolences to the families of victims in Friday's shooting, calling it a "heinous terrorist attack."
Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein called his Jordanian counterpart and "affirmed Iraq's solidarity with Jordan in the face of terrorism," Hussein's office said in a statement.

U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres condemned the attack during a funeral as "especially heinous," spokesman Stephane Dujarric said. "The secretary-general also calls for all those responsible to be found and to be held to account."

articles.headline: A 1,000-mile cloud on Mars may reveal physics never seen in nature
keyFacts: A 1,000-mile cloud forms and disappears near the Martian volcano Arsia Mons every morning during spring and summer.
Scientists recently modeled the cloud's formation for the first time using computer simulations.
Study lead author Jorge Hernández-Bernal said the results suggest the cloud is driven by theoretical physics never before observed in nature.
body: Every morning during the Martian spring and summer, a thin and extremely long cloud emerges, only to disappear again. The wispy formation appears near the volcano Arsia Mons and gradually elongates until it reaches over 1,000 miles—about the distance from New York to Kansas City as the crow flies—before dissipating. This cycle then repeats for several months.

Since it was first recorded by a probe in 2018, scientists have been unable to find a plausible explanation for the existence of this cloud, often referred to as the Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud (AMEC). Until now. Recently, researchers successfully modeled the cloud’s formation for the first time, their results suggesting that it may be driven by a physical process that has never been directly observed in any planet's atmosphere.

"We found that we needed to include some exotic physics… physics that, while included in textbooks, is treated as theoretical and usually thought not to happen in nature. It certainly hasn’t been seen in action before," Jorge Hernández-Bernal, a planetary scientist at Paris’ Sorbonne Université and lead author of the study, said in a press release . "Once we included this physics in our simulations, the AMEC emerged just as we hoped.”

articles.headline: Biden ‘autopen’ attorney and anti-Trump lawyer helping ‘Squad’ Rep. Ilhan Omar battle immigration probe
keyFacts: Attorneys Amy Jeffress and Joshua Matz are representing Representative Ilhan Omar amid an immigration and financial probe.
Federal agents searched Omar's Washington, D.C., home, prompting her lawyers to demand the return of her passport and seized electronics.
Former President Donald Trump called for Omar to immediately resign following the search and allegations regarding her immigration history.
body: The legal eagles defending embattled “Squad” Rep. Ilhan Omar from prison or deportation include former President Biden’s “autopen” personal attorney and the white-shoe lawyer who quarterbacked both of President Trump’s impeachments.

The Somalia-born Omar’s defense duo boasts impressive lefty legal pedigrees, but neither specializes in immigration law — raising questions about whether the Minnesota Democrat is more concerned about her husband’s alleged $30 million fraudulent windfall than she is about her immigration status.
Amy Jeffress, a partner at boutique DC firm Hecker Fink, became Biden’s personal attorney in 2025, succeeding longtime confidant Bob Bauer.
She represented the gaffe-prone former president as he faced investigations into his use of an autopen to sign presidential pardons and legislation.
A former attorney with DC firm Arnold & Porter, she played a role in some of the most intense partisan battles involving Congress.

She did outside work as counsel for the House Jan. 6 committee, helping push to haul in officials through subpoena authority. She previously represented former FBI lawyer Lisa Page — one of the “FBI lovers” who wrote anti-Trump texts during the 2016 presidential campaign that lead to accusations of “deep state” political bias and her eventual resignation.

The other half of Omar’s legal squad is Joshua Matz, also a partner at Hecker Fink, who represented House Democrats during both Trump impeachments and served on the legal team of the House Jan. 6. committee.

He also represented Brown University, New York University and Columbia University in legal battles involving Trump administration executive orders that promote merit by targeting affirmative action and diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) policies.

The probe into Omar’s immigration history and eyebrow-raising revisions to her financial disclosure forms is now being pursued by the US Attorney in DC, and comes as there was already deep suspicion around her in Congress, with financial questions persisting even after Omar amended her latest financial disclosure filings.

Omar, who claimed in an MS NOW interview that she lives “paycheck to paycheck” despite earning a $174,000 congressional salary, also said wasn’t allowed to phone her attorney for an hour after federal agents searched her home this month.

Court documents connected to the search of Omar’s DC home reference a prior alias, Nur Said Elmi — a detail that has drawn attention to investigators’ interest in her immigration history, due to allegations that first appeared on a Somali blog that ex husband Ahmed Nur Said Elmi is her brother.
“It is going to be a very expensive and challenging time and so we appreciate whether you’re able to send $5, $10, $20,” she said in the video Tuesday night.

Jeffress and Matz sent a seven-page letter to the Department of Justice last Friday, demanding the return of her passport, electronics and other seized property.
Trump, for his part, has made clear he intends to keep up the heat on Omar just as he has on some of Jeffress’ previous clients.
On Thursday night he called for her to “IMMEDIATELY” resign, saying she was sworn in under a different name different than her own.

articles.headline: Wales grind out frustrating WXV win against Japan
keyFacts: Wales defeated Japan 17-0 in tricky Tokyo conditions to secure their second victory of the WXV campaign.
Scrum-half Seren Lockwood scored two tries and Kelsey Jones added another for Wales during the match.
The two sides will play each other again in Kumagaya City on Saturday, 31 October.
body: - Published
WXV Global Series
Japan (0) 0
Wales (7) 17
Tries: Lockwood 2, K Jones Con: Bell
Wales ground out a win over Japan in tricky Tokyo conditions to secure a second victory of their WXV campaign.
Swirling wind, rain and humidity made for a real battle between sides ranked 11th and 12th in the world, with a scrappy first-half looking likely to end scoreless.
But scrum-half Seren Lockwood's 35th-minute snipe gave the game a much-needed spark and the visitors a 7-0 advantage at the break.

Wales lost centre Freya Bell to a serious-looking knee injury, but the impact of the bench proved the difference as Kelsey Jones drove over off lineout ball, before Lockwood finished a rare moment of class at the death.
It was far from an impressive performance from Sean Lynn's resurgent Wales, but given their previous results, his side have now proven the ability to win ugly.
The two sides will meet again in Kumagaya City on Saturday, 31 October.
Centenary celebrations dampened
The hosts, who were playing in a double header with the men's side to celebrate Japanese rugby's centenary, had twice run Ireland close before their meeting with Wales.
But indiscipline has been somewhat of an Achilles heel, and they lost flanker Nami Asari to a yellow card just six minutes into the Test.

Wales looked to have taken immediate advantage from a five-metre lineout, with Jones peeling away to cross for what would have been her ninth international try, but on review, lock Jorja Aiono was deemed to have caused an obstruction.
Japan hit back with some attacking phases of their own, with Bell and Sisilia Tuipulotu combining well to hold prop Wako Kitano up over the line.
Wales continued to look comfortable in defence as Japan patiently went through the phases, but the visitors' renewed attacking prowess looked disjointed amid wayward kicks and handling errors.
It was disappointing considering Wales' 74-point haul in their previous two outings against South Africa and USA, but then conditions were not in their favour.
The breakthrough eventually came five minutes before the break, and it was again off a driving lineout.
The powerful Bell trucked the ball up to the line, with Lockwood quick to the breakdown and quick to spot a gap in the defence.
Bell added the conversion to end the half.
Bell injury blow
Japan came back out with much more attacking intent and looked more threatening as Wales began to slip off tackles.
Lynn's side were also dealt a blow when a distraught-looking Bell was stretchered off the pitch, but there was an able replacement waiting in Courtney Keight.

Lleucu George was also introduced before the hour mark as Wales looked to win back some territory, and the backline reshuffle paid off when they added a second try on a rare visit to Japan's 22 on 65 minutes.
And this time there was no denying Jones at the back of the driving maul, with Wales putting some distance between themselves and their hosts.
They looked to have added an immediate third try when Lockwood won the chase from Keira Bevan's hack through, but replays showed Jones' turnover in the build-up had been from an offside position.
Lockwood did, however, bag her second three minutes from time, with the makeshift wing finishing well after George's floating pass out wide.
Wales pushed for a try bonus-point with Nami Yoshida sin-binned, but had to settle for three to go with a first clean sheet since beating Hong Kong 65-0 in November 2018.

articles.headline: Raspberry Pi Desktop proves old PCs aren't past it
keyFacts: The Register reported that Raspberry Pi Desktop has been updated to the Debian 13-based PiOS 6.3 release for x86-64 PCs.
The Register stated that the operating system performed well on old hardware, such as a 2008 ThinkPad X200s and a 2007 ThinkPad X61 Tablet.
The Register concluded that the system provides a lightweight, beginner-friendly alternative for old PCs and unsupported Intel Macs.
body: One of the most frequently asked questions of Linux folks is "what's the best lightweight distro for an old PC?" The Reg FOSS desk's current answer is Raspberry Pi Desktop.

A couple of weeks ago, we covered the news of a Trixie update for the Raspberry Pi Desktop . Since then, we've been putting it through its paces on a couple of the oldest, slowest machines in the FOSS desk stables. It has performed splendidly.

If you fancy dipping a tentative toe into Linux, but you only have a relatively old low-spec PC spare to try it on, this is ideal. This is a modern OS: it's a 2.6 GB download, and it uses about 8 GB of disk space when installed. It will be a bit too much for a 25-year-old PC that was intended for Windows XP, but if you have an old PC from the Windows Vista era to hand, that should do.

The splash screen calls it "PiOS 6.3," just as on Arm-based Raspberry Pi hardware. Here, though, we're testing Raspberry Pi Desktop: the x86-64 PC edition of the Debian-based system, available at the bottom of the downloads page .

Back in 2023, the PiOS got a new Debian 12-based version , which included a new Wayland-based desktop – although it still looked almost identical to the old environment, based on X11, Openbox, and LXDE. Sadly, the PC version didn't get upgraded. Two years later – so, almost exactly a year ago – we got a Debian 13-based PiOS 6 . The PC version still didn't get upgraded.

Now the PC edition has finally caught up with Debian 13. It's very similar to September's PiOS 6.3 release, complete with the option of a dock instead of a taskbar. Like the Arm version, you can use the raspi-config tool to switch between the Wayland-based labwc compositor and X.org if you prefer.

There is one important difference: Raspberry Pi OS still offers 32-bit and 64-bit Arm editions, but Raspberry Pi Desktop is now x86-64 only, following Debian 13's retirement of its x86-32 edition . The Arm editions now use kernel 6.18 , but the PC version is still on Debian's default kernel 6.12.

It brings the Pi's streamlined Debian desktop to PCs, with an installer that asks few technical questions. You can do a custom installation into existing partitions if you want, but you can just click "OK" a few times and it will do almost everything for you automatically. Unlike Debian itself, there are no questions about what to download, which desktop, network installation, or anything like that. One size fits all.

You get a custom desktop with a broadly Windows 95-style layout, except that the taskbar is at the top of the screen (you can move it if you want). You get a basic collection of preinstalled apps: Chromium, Firefox, a text editor, and some helpful documentation – albeit aimed at owners of real Pi hardware. At idle, it runs in a little under 450 MB of memory, and if you switch to X.org, Openbox uses about 50 MB less. The lightest variant of Ubuntu is generally agreed to be Lubuntu, but PiOS takes about half as much memory as Lubuntu 26.04 did in our testing .

We tried it on a ThinkPad X200s, released in 2008 . Ours has been upgraded with 8 GB of RAM, plus a spare 128 GB SATA SSD, but it's on the original 1.86 GHz Core 2 Duo SL9400 and Intel GMA4500 integrated GPU. Everything we tested worked, including Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Ethernet, USB 2, volume control buttons, brightness keys, and an external screen on DisplayPort. It automatically picked up and added our network printer, and happily connected to both 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz Wi-Fi networks.

For something even older and lower end, we went back to the year Vista was released: 2007 . We transplanted the SSD into a ThinkPad X61 Tablet from that same year. Our very battered X61 has 2 GB of DDR2 RAM. PiOS handled that fine – with the sole exception of the touchscreen, which didn't work. (We've only ever got that working with Windows XP.)

In a 19-year-old PC with an SSD, PiOS booted in under half a minute, and it was able to run Firefox and Chromium and go online. Pages rendered slowly, but it worked. On the better-specced X200s, with four times the RAM, even the web experience was tolerable, if you're patient. We also tried it on a high-end machine from 2008, a Thinkpad W500, complete with AMD GPU. On that, it feels positively snappy.

In our testing, PiOS takes as little memory as Alpine with Xfce – but it's far easier to install. Because it's Debian, it was also much easier to get additional apps such as both text-mode and GUI WordPerfect for Linux working. With Wine 11 from WineHQ , Microsoft Office 97 installed and ran superbly too.
If you're willing to trade a tiny bit of security for visibly better performance, the tweaks we gave in 2022 still work well.

PiOS is about as frugal as ChromeOS Flex, but you don't need a Google account or any other cloud login, and you get all-you-can-eat local apps. Compared to middleweight distros such as Linux Mint Xfce, Linux Lite, MX Linux, or Lubuntu, PiOS is significantly less demanding of hardware resources.

There are even lighter-weight Linuxes out there. For example, there is a Debian 13 version of antiX Linux , but although smaller, it has an overwhelming collection of kernels, init systems, window managers, and file managers. AntiX is not beginner-friendly. In 2024, we l ooked at Tiny Core Linux 15 , which is far smaller. Now up to version 17.1, it remains a specialist tool: you'll need serious tech skills to add extra apps, let alone update.

Alpine is capable, versatile, and lightweight, but assembling a desktop requires considerably more work. If you take the time to learn your way around it, Alpine can be configured to use even less disk and memory than PiOS, but Alpine has a smaller selection of software than Debian – unless you add Flatpak, which negates Alpine's lightweight, clean simplicity. Experienced Debian or Devuan users could build something leaner, but Raspberry Pi Desktop saves them the trouble. Its team has had 14 years of practice in diet Debian.

The Raspberry Pi Desktop also supports Intel Mac hardware, and it's ideal for old-but-working Macs now long-unsupported by macOS. It could also suit older Intel MacBooks whose RAM can't be expanded, although Wi-Fi, graphics, and other hardware support will depend on the model. A 4 GB MacBook Air may still have useful life running current browsers and LibreOffice. Just possibly not at the same time.

This should be your go-to option for an old, low-spec PC. It won't make a 15-year-old computer as fast as a new one. But it can make a 15-year-old PC useful again, with current, supported apps and tools. Once you get familiar with PiOS on a low-end x86 machine, it will also work fine on newer and more capable hardware. ®

articles.headline: VZMORE AX9 Max AI mini PC review
keyFacts: TechRadar reviewed the VZMORE AX9 Max AI mini PC, which features an AMD Ryzen AI 9 HX 470 processor, dedicated NPU, and robust connectivity options.
Reviewers found that the machine delivers strong CPU benchmark performance and handles creative apps, office work, and moderate gaming well, though its 32GB RAM and 1TB SSD limit heavier workloads.
The mini PC is available now, starting at $1,349 from VZMore and online retailers like Amazon.
body: TechRadar Verdict

At the top end of standard form-factor mini PCs, the AX9 Max, with its Ferrari-styled logo, it promises speed, luxury, and exceptional performance. Sure enough, the full metal casing, powerful processing engines, and detailing all add up. It features AMD Ryzen AI 9 HX 470 graphics and a dedicated NPU to maximise its AI potential. SSD and RAM upgrades also offer plenty of flexibility, so the platform can expand with your needs. However, if you want it to meet its full potential, then that comes at a hefty price.
Reasons to buy
- + Excellent CPU benchmark performance.
- + Fast SSD performance.
- + Plenty of connectivity options.
Reasons to avoid
- - Premium pricing.
- - Integrated graphics limit demanding GPU workloads.
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
VZMORE AX9 Max AI: 30-second review

The AX9 Max instantly feels premium, with a full metal build and a huge array of ports on the front and back. However, as you look closely at the embossed detailing around the edges and a logo that seems to blend the old Cadillac and Ferrari logos, something about the aesthetics starts to looks a little less premium.

Aesthetics aside, the build quality is solid enough and well finished, with the most impressive aspect being the sheer volume of ports that have been fitted around the exterior. On the front, there’s a selection of USB Type-A ports and the usual headphone jack; around the back, there are even more connectivity options, including two USB4 ports.

To handle the potential power draw of the devices you can hook up to the box, it packs a powerful AMD Ryzen AI 9 HX 470 processor which is supplied with the 120W power supply. The processor is relatively new, launched at the start of 2026, so it has had a good amount of time to bed in and now has a proven track record. This is supported by an integrated GPU and a dedicated NPU for all those new AI workloads.

As the test progressed, the machine's speed in Microsoft Office apps and the Adobe Creative Suite highlighted its potential. During video editing, the internal SSD kept pace with high-resolution edits without issue. However, a little more headroom on the 1TB capacity would have been beneficial.

Storage and RAM are the two interesting points of this machine. While both are modest in my review sample, maxing them out could turn this from a powerful mini PC into something that will hold great interest for anyone looking to run offline AI and larger LLMs, although that potential does come at a huge monetry cost.

Throughout the test, the creative applications and handling of video and image files were limited by the 32GB of RAM and 1TB SSD. However, with two USB4 ports, I could at least boost the storage capacity. For most HD and 4K edits, the machine handled rough cuts and transitions in Premiere Pro quickly and without issue, though more RAM would have helped.

The most interesting test was running LM Studio and a few local models; while general performance was good, especially for models that utilised the NPU, I could see where the 32GB RAM limit restricted what the machine could potentially do, limiting it as the best mini PC specifically for AI workloads.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!

For gaming, at mid settings in most games like Cyberpunk 2077 and Indiana Jones and the Great Circle, the machine was more than capable of supplying the power needed for the action. However, again, a little more RAM would have smoothed some of the minor slowdowns in gameplay, especially in Cyberpunk 2077 where quality settings had to be lowered.

This is a machine with potential, and while undoubtedly expensive for a mini PC with a 1TB SSD and 32GB RAM, that money is invested in that powerful CPU, GPU and NPU combo and the ability to expand the storage to a far greater degree than I have seen on the vast majority of other mini PCs of this size and type.
VZMORE AX9 Max AI: Price and availability
- How much does it cost? From $1,349
- When is it out? Available now
- Where can you get it? Directly from VZMore and online retailers.
At present, the UK price is £1,349 for the 32GB RAM and 1TB SSD configuration I’m looking at in this review.
At the time of review, the US site is down (maybe it's just me?), however, it's available on Amazon for $1,399.
- Value: 4 / 5
VZMORE AX9 Max AI: Specs
Processor: AMD Ryzen AI 9 HX 470
Graphics: AMD Radeon 890M
NPU: AMD Ryzen AI, up to 55 TOPS
Memory: 32GB DDR5
Storage: 1TB PCIe 4.0 SSD
Operating System: Windows 11 Pro
Front ports: 5 × USB 3.2 Gen 2 Type-A, 3.5mm Audio
Rear ports: 2 × USB4, USB 3.2 Gen 2 Type-A, USB 2.0 Type-A, 2 × HDMI 2.1, 2 × 2.5Gb Ethernet
Wireless: Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 5.4
Card Reader: SD 4.0
Power Modes: Silent 45W, Balanced 54W, Performance 65W
Dimensions: Approx. 134.9 × 131.8 × 57.7mm
Weight: 777.5g
Power Adapter: 120W
VZMORE AX9 Max AI: Design

Unpacking the compact AX9 Max, the metal casing and detailed plastic base of this mini PC instantly reinforced its price point. Only after carefully checking the detailing and the large, shiny logo on top did I start to question whether this was a premium machine or just one trying to look premium.

Checking the specifications and that the price point was justified, but there’s still something about the design that feels a little over the top. The rest of the design is solid, and at 134.9 × 131.8 × 57.7mm and 777.5g, it’s a great size and weight for this style of machine.

Around the casing, there are four USB 3.2 Gen 2 Type-A ports and a 3.5mm stereo headphone jack. On the left side of the casing is an SD 4.0 memory card slot, while the back has two USB4 Type-C ports, a USB 2.0 port, two HDMI 2.1 ports, two 2.5Gb RJ45 sockets, a USB 3.2 Gen 2 Type-A port, and the DC-in port.

Despite the number of ports, they’re well laid out, and testing with multiple accessories, SSDs, and other card readers showed the port selection offered enough space to easily plug in and remove cables when needed.

You access the inner workings of the mini PC through the base, and while it's designed to be upgraded, initial access proved tricky, but only because of the four small rubber plugs covering the screw holes.
Once these are removed, removing the base is easy, and thankfully there are no easily detachable wires to get in the way of speedy progress.
- Design: 4 / 5
VZMORE AX9 Max AI: Features

The aesthetics of this machine are quite run-of-the-mill despite the premium metal build. However, as I checked the specifications, I found plenty that’s quite exciting. First, it features the AMD Ryzen AI 9 HX 470 with 12 cores and 24 threads, plus Radeon 890M integrated graphics. That’s a powerful combo, especially with the dedicated NPU rated at 55 TOPS.

To keep up with this processing power, the machine has a substantial cooling system; flip it over, and the base design suddenly makes sense, as it, along with the huge venting on the back, is designed to keep the machine cool.

VZMORE has its own cooling system called V-Cooling, which uses a vapour chamber and a 360º air intake on the base, and the company claims it provides 65W of sustained TDP output while keeping things quiet. In testing, this claim held up: the cooling seemed effective and quiet for the most part until it was put under heavy load and even then while the fans are audible they’re still well managed.
As mini PCs go, one of the first notable features is the sheer volume of ports across the body. This is far more than most, with wireless connection options including Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 5.4.
There are also three selectable power modes, including 45W Silent mode, 54W Balanced and 65W Performance. Through this test, I turned it to Performance mode.

This machine is aimed at creatives, those looking to use AI and gamers- all high-demand applications. As I reviewed the specifications, a couple of points stood out. First, the internal SSD was limited to 1TB in the review sample, and given the machine's price, I expected at least 2TB.

The other point is that the SSD is PCIe Gen 4 x4, which still provides plenty of speed, as I saw in the benchmarks, but I would have expected an upgrade to PCIe Gen 5. The other point is that there are two M.2 slots: one pre-installed with an M.2 2280 module and one M.2 2230, slot that can only take up to 1TB. That’s still 5TB in a relatively small box, but for this price, I would have expected a little more.
the main point here is that CPU, GPU and NPU combo is an expensive choice and that’s what you’re paying for here.

Then comes the real surprise, the RAM. This is 32GB of DDR5 SO-DIMM, split into dual-channel. That in itself isn't unusual, but since AI is one of the machine's key selling points, this 32GB can be upgraded to 256GB. However, at the time of writing, the most that I could find was 128GB in two 64GB modules for the cool price of £1,999. This could be possible, but would you really want it?
In this test, I’ve run Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and Gemma-4-26B-A4B through LM Studio.

The machine arrives with Windows 11 Pro pre-installed and only needs the final steps of the installation to be completed. However, this takes a good 10–15 minutes, rejecting each of the many packages on offer. Once in, Windows 11 Pro runs smoothly, and the Microsoft Office suite is fast, as is interaction with Windows as a whole. Word, Excel, and PowerPoint are all well within its capabilities.

Moving on to Photoshop and Lightroom, the machine's power is evident, but the limits of 32GB of RAM are quickly apparent. The applications load quickly, and photos load into Photoshop and Lightroom are easily adjusted. It’s only when I do batch updates in Lightroom or select files in Adobe Bridge that I started to notice the limitations. On a machine at this price, I really expected a little more performance, and checking the Device Monitor showed the RAM topping out.

Again, loading Premiere Pro and some HD and 4K video, the initial HD footage ran smoothly, with the AX9 Max handling the video files with ease. 4K video was handled just as well, but again, RAM limits meant that as the edit grew more complex, it was best to give the machine a few seconds to catch up with the renders. Still, a good 5-minute 4K edit is well within the limits, and again it’s the RAM that holds the machine back. Another point was that I needed to connect an external SSD to one of the USB4 ports because of limited storage.

Overall, the machine is exceptional for heavy office use and more than able to keep up with the demands. What stood out was how easy it was to connect multiple accessories and screens, thanks to the port support around the case.
For creative applications, the machine performed well and handled most task with relative ease, although I would definitely boost the RAM to 64GB for video work.

To really test the machine’s potential, I loaded Indiana Jones and the Great Circle and was pleased to see that, with settings at moderate, it was more than capable of delivering smooth gameplay and stunning graphics. However, when I switched to Cyberpunk 2077, the gameplay faltered, and I had to dig into the settings and dial everything back to near-base levels to get the smooth gameplay I prefer.

The final test was to run a few LLMs locally and run a series of tests on the machine. The results here were mixed as I switched between two models, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and Gemma-4-26B-A4B. On the initial run, I noticed that as the five tests I ran, technical writing, programming, reasoning, image understanding, and review analysis, became more intensive, the machine slowed down and the available RAM maxed out.

Using the installed models in LM Studio provided decent performance, with the chat flowing easily and responses coming back relatively quickly, in 2 to 5 seconds. However, as complexity rose, so did processing times and machine noise.

First, with every request, RAM maxed out between 95% and 99%, leaving little, if any, headroom for the machine to do anything else. The first test, writing a short 200-word technical piece with the Qwen model, took 4.38 seconds to get the first response, at 19.1 tokens per second, requiring 5920 output tokens, for a total run time of 316.7 seconds. Far slower than online models, but still all done completely offline.
Less complex models completed this task far faster, with less finesse in the wording.

Running a Python coding task to read and organise a folder of image files, again using the Qwen model, maxed out the machine across the board, with the fans kicking in to keep things cool. Time to first token was just over 1 second, with 18.84 tokens per second; 7653 output tokens took 407.36 seconds to complete the task. This was more impressive as the folder contained 2,764 images. The Python script could then be run to create a CSV file containing the file information. This is base-level organisation.
As I started pushing more complex image-analysis models, the machine's limits were hit, with processing times running in excess of ten minutes, mainly due to limited RAM.
However, the local LLMs available in LM Studio are surprisingly good, but they aren’t a replacement for online or higher-end models.
- Performance: 4 / 5
VZMORE AX9 Max AI: Final verdict

The VZMORE AX9 Max AI Mini PC is a powerful mini PC with plenty of potential and a premium build. The aesthetics and large logo on top feel a little out of place for a machine at this price and for its intended audience; I usually associate that type of styling with entry-level models.

It is undoubtedly a powerful machine with a CPU, GPU and NPU that make light work of most Copilot and app-initiated AI tasks, and even with 32GB of RAM, it handles all office and most creative tasks without issue. What surprised me was that it struggled with some AI processing through LM Studio, with longer-than-expected processing times because the 32GB limit pushed the RAM to near 100% for extended periods.

Likewise, while most games played back smoothly, Cyberpunk 2077 struggled with the graphics, and the quality options and resolution had to be dropped to get smooth gameplay. Other games, such as Indiana Jones and the Great Circle, played well.

Creative use was also mixed, again held back by that 32GB of RAM, which topped out in Premiere Pro, causing slight slowdowns when editing 4K Log footage. Editing standard 4K and HD was fast, though I still needed to attach an external SSD to expand storage.

The point is that the machine supports up to 256GB of RAM, far more than I’ve seen in any other mini PC. However, as I couldn’t find 128GB modules in the UK, and the maximum available at this time is 2 × 64GB, costing between £1,500 and £2,000, this value seems to be theoretical rather than a reality.

As it is, this is a powerful mini PC, but while it offers upgrade options and plenty of connectivity, it feels like it overpromises; to reach its full potential, you’ll need to invest more in upgrades. At present what makes this machine the price it is, is that CPU, and in order for you to see it’s full potential this machine needs far more investment.
Should I buy the VZMORE AX9 Max AI?
Buy it if...
You need a compact PC with CPU performance.
The AMD CPU, GPU and NPU combine to offer impressive performance across the board.
You need high-speed external connectivity.
With dual USB4 and LAN, you get plenty of fast and standard connectivity options.
Don't buy it if...
You need a dedicated GPU for demanding graphics or 3D workloads.
The USB4 port lets you connect to an eGPU, but if you need that processing contained in this small box, this won’t be the solution.
You need local AI performance.
To reach its potential, you’ll need to invest in additional RAM, which is incredibly expensive.

articles.headline: Canada is feeling the pain from Trump's tariffs — but the trade fight didn't start overnight
keyFacts: President Trump's U.S. tariffs on Canadian goods are squeezing Canada's economy, threatening jobs, and raising consumer prices.
Experts say the trade fight stems from long-standing disputes over dairy and other products under agreements like the USMCA.
Higher energy prices have combined with the tariffs to add further financial pressure on consumers.
body: President Donald Trump's escalating trade fight with Canada is squeezing the economy north of the border, threatening jobs and adding to families' financial strain as steep U.S. tariffs on roughly $20 billion in goods remain in place.

U.S. tariffs have hammered the country's steel, aluminum, lumber and automobile producers that depend heavily on the American market. Steel exports have fallen by roughly half since the tariffs took effect, while lumber exports were about 20% below 2024 levels earlier this year, according to the Bank of Canada . Production and jobs have also declined in some of the hardest-hit industries.

Canadian families are feeling the squeeze, too. Consumer prices were 3% higher in August than a year earlier, with grocery prices up 2.8% and transportation costs jumping 7.5%, according to the government's own data .
A MUST-WIN MIDTERM STATE IS THE REAL LOSER OF TRUMP'S CANADA TRADE WAR
Retaliatory tariffs on American products have also added to those costs.

Prices of affected goods, which includes groceries, household products, furniture, electronics and appliances, rose roughly 6% more than comparable products that were not hit by the tariffs, according to the country's central bank.
But while Canada is feeling the economic pain, the disputes driving Trump's trade fight are not new.

"The Trump administration is complaining about dairy access and, generally speaking, those complaints are completely valid," David Clement, North American affairs manager at the Consumer Choice Center, told Fox News Digital.
"Canada has exorbitant tariffs on imports from the United States and really from everywhere around the world when it comes to chicken, turkey, eggs, cheese and milk," Clement said.
THE OVERLOOKED WAY THE IRAN WAR IS MAKING GROCERIES, AMAZON PACKAGES AND NEW HOMES MORE EXPENSIVE

Clement noted, however, that differences between American and European access to Canada's market reflect terms negotiated under separate trade agreements, including the USMCA struck during Trump's first term.
But dairy represents just a fraction of the broader U.S.-Canada trading relationship.

Scott Lincicome, vice president of general economics at the Cato Institute and the Herbert A. Stiefel Center for Trade Policy Studies, said more than 99% of U.S.-Canada trade was duty-free before 2025, with negotiators historically willing to tolerate disputes over politically sensitive products like dairy to preserve the broader relationship.
"The Trump administration has so far refused to make the deal," he said.
Lincicome said free trade in products including fertilizer, energy and lumber helps keep costs down for American farmers, homebuilders and consumers.
With the midterm elections just weeks away and the cost of living in focus, the trade dispute is unfolding as higher energy prices add another layer of pressure on consumers.
Lincicome called the combination a "double whammy."
"First you had the tariffs which increased the prices of a lot of products. And then you had energy prices spike because of the Iran war," he said.

Higher diesel prices can ripple through the economy because they fuel tractors, trucks and trains, Lincicome said, acting "as kind of another tariff" by raising the cost of getting products to consumers.
Despite the escalating tensions, Clement cautioned against allowing the dispute to undermine the broader relationship.

"The partnership between Canada and the United States is one of the greatest trading relationships the world has ever known," he said. "That should be embraced. It should be enhanced, and it shouldn't be torn down by either side."

articles.headline: America, You Can’t Get This Powerhouse Phone. It’s a Shame
keyFacts: Oppo launched its Find X10 and Find X10 Pro photography-focused smartphones in Spain, which is the company's largest European market.
Oppo and other Chinese smartphone-makers are avoiding the US market due to geopolitical roadblocks and a lack of carrier relationships, analysts said.
Oppo plans to increase its investment in its European business by 30% over the next three years, according to the company.
body: If the only two names that pop into your head when you think about the best phones on the market are Apple and Samsung, frankly, you’re thinking too small.

Chinese phone-makers aren’t just making phones that rival those from Apple and Samsung; in some respects, they’re surpassing the iPhones and Galaxys — in batteries and fast charging, and especially when it comes to cameras.

On Wednesday, Oppo launched its latest photography-focused high-end phones, the Find X10 and Find X10 Pro, on the sun-bleached Spanish island of Mallorca. A finca covered in bougainvillea and surrounded by gnarled olive groves and roving wild goats might at first glance seem like an offbeat choice for a Chinese tech giant to stage a global launch event, but the decision is far from random. Spain is Oppo’s biggest European market, and it’s only getting bigger.
More from CNET

It’s a story we’re seeing repeat itself around the world. According to researchers Counterpoint and Omdia, Oppo was the fourth-largest phone-maker globally by shipments in the first half of this year. Already well established in China, the company is now seeing growth across the globe, and in Europe in particular.

It’s an impressive feat given that growing a smartphone business is harder than it’s ever been. It’s no secret that RAMageddon, the ongoing memory shortage, is pushing up phone prices and causing a massive drop in shipments.

Phone-makers might be putting on a brave face as they release new devices to the world, but behind the scenes they’re scrambling to draw up new strategies that will hopefully see them through in both the short and long term.

Growing sales of flagship and premium phones will be key to their survival, said Runar Bjorhovde, principal analyst at market research firm Omdia, during a briefing at the Oppo event. Compared with the budget and midrange segments, the high-end segment is relatively resilient.

You might think that means more exciting (if expensive) phones everywhere – witness the launch of Apple’s folding iPhone Duo, which starts at $1,999 – particularly in wealthy countries such as the US. But that’s not exactly the case.
Bad news for US phone buyers
When it comes to premium phone markets, none is larger or more profitable than the US. And yet Oppo and other Chinese smartphone-makers are steering well clear.

There are several reasons for this. Firstly, they don’t have Apple’s and Samsung’s long-standing carrier relationships that would facilitate their phones being presented as solid options to buyers. Together with the geopolitical roadblocks affecting Chinese tech companies, this makes the US simply too tricky and precarious right now to make that investment worthwhile.

“The barriers to enter make it almost impossible to go in and actually scale there unless you have lots of money to invest,” said Bjorhovde. Instead, the money they do have to invest is being poured into Europe. (Oppo said it will increase its investment in its European business by 30% over the next three years.)

This is bad news for Americans, who simply don’t and won’t be able to benefit from the full array of choices on offer to people in Europe and beyond, including the Find X10 Pro. In CNET’s review of the device, Editor at Large Andrew Lanxon described it as “a powerhouse phone that’s well worthy of its flagship title,” praising its cameras as the best on the market alongside the iPhone 18 Pro and Xiaomi’s Leitzphone.
Of these three, only one is on sale in the US, but Europeans can take their pick.

“It definitely feels like US consumers are missing out by not having the latest and greatest smartphones from the leading Chinese manufacturers,” said Ben Wood, chief analyst at FDM CCS. It’s especially noticeable when it comes to some of the cutting-edge foldable phones from companies like Honor, Oppo and Xiaomi, he added.
Breaking the duopoly
The Apple-Samsung duopoly that dominates the American market also exists in Europe, albeit to a lesser extent. But Elvis Zhou, Oppo’s European CEO, wants to see it broken completely.

“People deserve more exciting options,” he said in a briefing with journalists. When it comes to picking a premium phone, he thinks people should have a choice between three or four brands, rather than just two.

This reflects the more diverse array of successful phone brands in China, he added. In his company’s home country, there are only a few percentage points difference between Huawei, Apple, Oppo, Vivo, Xiaomi and Honor.

Xiaomi, Honor and Vivo are all now vying with Oppo for a slice of the European pie. One sign of intensifying competition is the shrinking gap between products being launched in China and Europe, which has historically spanned months. Zhou says that’s changing — the Find X10 series launched in China only a month ago.

When it comes to choosing a premium phone, Omdia’s research shows that buyers place more importance on camera quality than do people buying budget and midrange devices, but also “softer” values, including preferred brand, perceived status and aesthetics. Oppo has nailed its camera system, but the same isn’t necessarily true of the latter values.

Zhou isn’t worried, though. Oppo is squarely targeting Gen Z with the Find X10 series (Omdia research shows that people under 35 are most likely to buy premium phones), and he thinks they’re savvy enough to look beyond ads to first-person recommendations and chatbots that will provide specs-based advice to discern which product will offer the best value.

“We want to focus on the young generation because … they know how to make the decision very logically – they will not make the decision only following the brand name,” he said. “Young people really care about the product itself, and they can get all the information they want from AI and from social media. It’s a good opportunity for me.”
The company has already found success using this strategy for the Find X9 series, which saw its share of the premium European market quadruple between 2025 and 2026, according to Omdia.

But while Oppo might have made headway in Europe, it might be difficult to sustain this effort over time, said Wood — especially given that all of its Chinese rivals are adopting a very similar strategy at the very same moment.
Competition might be fierce, but Oppo is ready to play the long game. “We’re very patient,” Zhou said with a wry smile. “We’re not rushing here in Europe.”
Editors’ note: Katie Collins’ travel costs were covered by Oppo. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.

articles.headline: What we've been playing - "Shoving Moon Flesh into an alien grandma's mouth"
keyFacts: Eurogamer staff members shared details about the video games they played recently in their weekly weekend feature article.
Bertie reported running a one-on-one Dungeons and Dragons mini-adventure called D8 Night with their partner.
Connor stated that Warframe players are currently participating in a limited-time event to feed Moon Flesh to an alien character for rewards.
body: 24th October

Hello, it is me, your regular weekend host Mertie and I am here once again to guide you gently into Saturday with our usual feature What We've Been Playing, where we write a little about the games we've been, yes, playing. This week, Bertie - before fleeing for a well-deserved break and leaving me with the keys to the place - runs a one-on-one D&D game; Connor plays with his Moon Flesh in Warframe, and I've been serenely gallivanting over yonder hills.

But enough about us, what about you? What have you been playing this week? Do tell all! And don't forget we have an entire archive of previous What We've Been Playings for your leisurely perusal, just in case you forgot what you were playing a year or a month or a week ago.
One-on-one Dungeons & Dragons, tabletop

I'm a little busy outside of work at the moment with rehearsals for a play I'm in (The Importance of Being Ernest), but I did find time for another Dungeons & Dragons first: a one-on-one game. I've been wanting to do one of these for a while, and, as I discovered recently, one-on-one games are a whole thing. Duets, they're called, rather poetically. You need to modify campaigns a bit to be playable this way, because most are designed for groups of four or five people, and you probably need to give a player a companion character as backup. But otherwise, it's totally doable. Some people make adventures exclusively for one-on-one games.

I ran a mini-adventure called D8 Night, created by the now-closed dice shop Dakota Irish. It's a nice, warm two-hour-or-so affair, where the player is caught in a time-stilled village and tasked by some magical mischief maker to retrieve the components of a romantic meal before being allowed to leave. It's a simple enough set-up, and as with a lot of things D&D, the set-up doesn't really matter so much as the playing of it and the unexpected things that happen. And unexpected things did happen. I played with my partner so I know her likes pretty well, I like to think - that's the attraction of a one-on-one set-up like this - but I didn't expect her to connect so strongly with some of the incidental characters. This resulted in entire areas being imagined-to-life that weren't written on paper. The imagination never ceases to amaze me.

Anyway, I'm off to Comic Con this weekend to celebrate my birthday - it'll be my birthday when you're reading this. I'm off to geek-out about Critical Role and watch the new Laika animated film, and to stuff my face with food.
-Bertie
Over the Hill, PC

I had a lovely time playing developer Funselektor's Art of Rally follow-up Over the Hill last week, roaming its beautifully stylised wilderness expanses in my cheerful 4x4 so I could write some words about it all. But it clearly got its hooks into me, and I went on to spend pretty much my entire Saturday just pootling around the Canadian Valhallas, the Algerian desert, thoroughly transfixed by the tranquil rhythms of it all.

It really is a game for the curious - and the infinitely patient. As the old meme goes: See that mountain?, you can climb it. Just be prepared for a lot of slow-going, a lot of trial-and-error, and a lot of determination. But while it should be frustrating, the opposite somehow ends up being true, and it's easy to feel at peace in this striking wilderness, guitars strumming gentle encouragement as you become one with the world.
-Matt
Warframe, PS5

You haven't experienced FOMO until you've experienced MMO do-this-or-you'll-never-be-able-to-do-it-again FOMO: The once-in-a-lifetime grinds, the cosmetics that may be vaguely impressive to onlookers in a decade's time, and the first-thing-in-the-morning, last-thing-at-night routines of logging on and doing busywork.

For those unaware, Warframe is currently bracing for a journey into a whole new galaxy. The trip requires fuel, but given we're talking about the big-red-number-loving, fashion-forward, weirdly wonderful Warframe here, this fuel isn't diesel. No, Warframe players in their thousands are currently shoving Moon Flesh into an alien grandma's mouth.

We're taking parts of Eris - a grim petri dish home to countless infested ghouls - and, fouler still, the Mesa warframe. Like a ripe cheese, its stink is what meemaw craves, and providing it brings great rewards. These include weapons and dead-handy consumables like Legendary Cores and Archon Shards, but perhaps more delectable are the cosmetics. Some must be unlocked through a community-wide effort, while others are available to buy with Moon Flesh from the jump. And, of course, once the event ends, these will never return. Never ever.

I've been waking up at 6am everyday and doing missions for this Moon Flesh, and I've been doing it before bed as well. I, like many hopeless MMO/-live service players, am petrified that something in the game may never be mine to hoard. It has cut into my gym time, my morning coffee time, and indeed my sleep time. I owe my recent spree of unsubtle yawns in morning team meetings to Warframe. That's either a glowing endorsement, or a sign I need to ease up on this stuff. Who knows?
-Connor
Nintendo Switch Sports Resort, Switch 2

Am I allowed two entries? I'm not actually sure, but Bertie's not here to stop me so... ALSO, I have found myself consumed by Switch Sports Resort this week in a way I absolutely wasn't expecting to be when I fired it up for review. In my head, Nintendo's long-running series has always very much been a party game first, and an engaging solo endeavour a distant second.

But Switch Sports Resort is a bit of a treasure, and I've been having a great time with it on my own: taking it online for a bit of ranked or casual play, working through some achievements, or just firing up one of its fantastic open-world sightseeing modes for a leisurely explore. I hope Nintendo's got some post-launch plans in the works, because I'd love for it to go a little bit harder with the open-world stuff, particularly where flying is concerned. But until then there's skateboarding, which is bloody brilliant, and I'm already craving more.
-Matt
