articles.headline: Avengers: Doomsday Promoted With Baseball-Themed Crossover Featuring MLB Players During World Series
keyFacts: Marvel Studios debuted a promotional crossover ad for Avengers: Doomsday featuring MLB players during Game 1 of the 2026 World Series.
The baseball-themed promo featured characters like Mr. Fantastic and The Thing before Dr. Doom attacked from the sky.
Avengers: Doomsday is scheduled to arrive in theaters everywhere on December 18.
body: Marvel Studios debuted a unique promo for Avengers: Doomsday during Game 1 of the 2026 World Series on Fox tonight between the Milwaukee Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays. The ad is an Avengers-MLB crossover set on Earth-828 at Ebbets Field (the former home of the Dodgers when they were in Brooklyn; it was torn down on our Earth in 1960 – the promo is seemingly set in the same time period as The Fantastic Four: First Steps, as you can see New York Giants players in the background).

In it, Mr. Fantastic, sporting a Brooklyn Dodgers cap, takes the mound to throw a stretchy-armed first pitch while The Thing hypes up the players as current, modern MLB players Freddie Freeman, Jacob Misiorowski, Bryce Harper, Randy Arozarena, and Junior Caminero look on from the sidelines. They're interrupted when Dr. Doom attacks from the sky, with clips from the film interspersed throughout the promo.

Worlds collide ⚾An exclusive preview of Marvel's new Avengers movie assembles Bryce Harper, Freddie Freeman, Jacob Misiorowski, Junior Caminero and Randy Arozarena 👀Avengers: Doomsday arrives in theaters everywhere December 18 https://t.co/WX1YtKjAKt

— MLB (@MLB) October 24, 2026 Live sporting events, such as the Super Bowl, NBA Finals, and World Series remain one of Hollywood's favorite mediums to debut new trailers and promote films, as in the age of streaming and on-demand content, they're one of the few forms of programming that consistently drive a live, tuned-in audience.

Avengers: Doomsday returns Chris Evans as Steve Rogers (which is referenced in a clip from the film used in the MLB promo), while Robert Downey Jr. trades Iron Man's mask for Dr. Doom's and appears to be abducting heroes in the upcoming film (though we will see RDJ as Stark at least one more time, starting in 2028 at Disney California Adventure's upcoming Avengers: Infinity Defense ride ). Much of it remains shrouded in mystery, such that even actors in the film don't know what happens .

Audience interest appears to be strong, as ticket pre-sales are outpacing those of this summer's blockbuster hit Spider-Man: Brand New Day. But Marvel recommends you do your homework before heading to the theater for Doomsday.

articles.headline: UK to invest £100m in 'world first' AI Biosecurity Lab
keyFacts: The UK government announced a 100 million pound investment in a national AI Biosecurity Lab to strengthen defences against biological threats.
AI Minister Kanishka Narayan stated the new lab will bring together scientific expertise to safeguard citizens from emerging risks.
OpenAI and Anthropic will support the lab by providing 200 million pounds worth of AI model credits.
body: - Published
The UK says it will establish a national AI Biosecurity Lab (AIBL) to help strengthen its defences against emerging biological threats.
As part of Wednesday's Budget, the government will commit Â£100m to establishing the new, "world first" institute with the support of leading AI firms.
The chancellor will also pledge millions of pounds in spending across a range of initiatives aimed at shoring up the UK's ability to respond to evolving cyber, biological and AI-enabled threats.
"AI will transform daily life: every firm, community, hospital, school, and every aspect of our economy can benefit," John Healey said.
"I understand and share the concerns of working people, so I am setting out a distinctively British approach to AI.
"One that doesn't leave workers behind and defends our national interest, while ensuring the benefits of AI-enabled growth are felt right across the country."
The full details about the role and remit of the new lab are yet to emerge.

But the AI Minister Kanishka Narayan said it would be a "major new global institution" that brings together "world-leading scientific expertise" to ensure the UK can safeguard its citizens and goals as AI develops.
"That means staying ahead of emerging threats, from cyber attacks to biological risks, while building more of the critical technology our security depends on," he said.
"By backing British science, advanced chips and our own AI companies, we can strengthen our national security, rebuild Britain's industrial strength and create good, skilled jobs across the country."
The AI Biosecurity Lab's creation will also be supported by leading AI developers, with OpenAI and Anthropic providing Â£200m worth of AI model credits that can be spent on the use of their models.
The Chancellor's plans to boost AI spending will also see an additional Â£120m committed to the UK's AI Security Institute (AISI).

Established by the former Conservative government in 2023, the lab evaluates the risks of the most advanced and powerful models - and has been championed for its role in helping build a collaborative and open approach to AI testing.

The additional funding announced by the Chancellor will aim to help ensure the lab can continue its efforts and work, particularly amid growing calls for technical standards and guardrails for AI development.

It will come alongside a Â£60m investment in what it coined a "National Cyber Shield" which it said would use agentic AI to boost cyber-defences, and Â£70m funding towards a National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre.
This, it said, would harness AI tools to detect cyber vulnerabilities across the UK's critical infrastructure and economy.

It comes after the UK government revealed it was among organisations around the world to have taken some sites offline as a precaution after critical flaws were surfaced in a popular programming language.

Researchers who helped surface the vulnerabilities in PHP - a popular server-side scripting language used in web development for decades - warned platforms which use it could be exposed to potential hacks.
There have been no reports of any successful exploits of the flaw, coined php2shell, so far.
But experts have warned that the incident shows how quickly and easily bugs which have lain long dormant may be surfaced - and potentially exploited - using AI.

articles.headline: Startups don’t need to go viral to win customers
keyFacts: At TechCrunch Disrupt, industry leaders discussed strategies for startups to attract and retain early customers without relying solely on viral social media.
Gamma CEO Grant Lee stated that influencer marketing requires targeted creators and deep collaboration rather than a passive, set-it-and-forget-it approach.
Engine founder Elia Wallen and Google Ventures partner Crystal Huang emphasized that traditional offline sales tactics and analyzing user data are also effective.
body: Getting initial customers as a startup can be one of the most grueling challenges in business. Even when companies manage to snag some early interest, there’s no guarantee those customers will stick around.

At TechCrunch Disrupt last week, Elia Wallen, founder and CEO of travel startup Engine, Gamma founder and CEO Grant Lee, and Crystal Huang, general partner at Google Ventures, shared tips on how to attract and retain customers.

In the current era — when young AI companies like Cluely and Instinct are building big audiences not just through their products but also through their founders’ colorful online presences — social media can seem like a magic bullet for reaching early customers. But founders who want heighten their business strategy with modern marketing, have to be strategic, according to Lee.

Gamma, which sells AI-powered presentation software, managed to scale its business exponentially with a social media strategy that deployed influencers through its Ambassadors (or “Gambassador”) program. The company adopted the plan before influencer-based marketing was a tried-and-true strategy for smaller companies, eventually reaching a multi-billion dollar valuation.
But simply giving influencers a platform and telling them to promote your brand online doesn’t automatically translate to sales, said Lee. There’s more to it than that.

“If you have a product that can serve many different segments or use cases, then you want to basically have creators that can target each one of those,” Lee said. “If you have folks that are in consulting versus people that do all their marketing and create all the decks for their CMO, there’s all these different segments you might want to go after.”
Lee said sometimes founders seem to treat creator marketing or influencer marketing as a sort of set it and forget it thing.

“I think you’re better served by really spending a lot of time with these creators, because if they’re not able to understand how to articulate the value of your product, it doesn’t matter how much money you spend, it’s just going to fall flat,” Lee added.
The effectiveness of social media depends largely on the type of business. Other ways of reaching customers can be just (if not more) effective.

Wallen would know. His company Engine, which manages lodging and travel bookings for midsize businesses, bootstrapped its way to $150 million in bookings before taking on any outside funding. They also had no visible social media strategy at all. For Wallen, traditional sales tactics can be far more useful than a positive TikTok video.

“We did events and we smiled and dialed,” said Wallen. “We still have a lot of people picking up the phone. A lot of people who didn’t grow up with that or don’t understand it think that it’s outdated or it doesn’t work but it does. It’s a hard thing. There are a lot of companies that just refuse to do it or don’t know how to do it well. But they’re missing out on a very big offline client base.” He added: “The phone still works.”

Wallen also shared an in-person tactic that his company deployed during its scrappy early days: hiring a magician named David to perform tricks for prospective clients at events and encourage them to visit the Engine’s booth. In short, old-fashioned personal engagement can work just as well, if not better, than the latest social media tricks.
Huang, who has managed droves of startups and shepherded them to success, said that once you have a customer, a lot of value can be derived from looking at how they use the product.

“Can you look into usage data and figure out if it’s recurring, if it’s increasing, if they are referring their friends?” Huang said. “It can come across in early usage and retention information as well. And then also, do you see some super fans, right, who even want to work at the company, promote the company, be attached to the brand?” She added: “You need to have ways to create evangelists who are really passionate about the product.”

articles.headline: Belmont’s Curse Taught Me An Important Lesson About Parrying, Namely I Should Do It More
keyFacts: Kotaku reported that the video game Belmont’s Curse features overwhelming combat scenarios with numerous hazards and projectiles.
The author stated they struggled to defeat the boss Mammon using their preferred ranged and avoidant playstyle.
The author discovered that using the parry mechanic, as seen in professional speedruns, allowed them to finally defeat the boss.
body: Belmont’s Curse is not for the easily overwhelmed. At any given time, the game requires me to track rooms full of arrows, laser beams, axes, icicles, boulders, and birds, any one of which could be hurtling toward my person and often all of them are at once. Thankfully, protagonist Rose Belmont has been gifted with an arsenal of tools to assist her deadly travels in Casa de Dracula, but again: overwhelmed. After a certain point, there are too many tools to keep track of and I just fall back on the ones that have worked the best for me. But one thing I’ve appreciated about my time with Belmont’s CurseÂ is how it’s forced me out of that comfort zone.

I typically favor a ranged playstyle, preferring the spear and whip weapons because with them I can keep a healthy distance and still dish out pain. Movement tools like the air dash, thorn whip, and slide help on the defense side and I’ve come to rely on them almost exclusively. For me, the best and easiest way to avoid damage is to simply get the hell away from the damage. With this avoidant strategy, I’ve been having a pretty decent time until one boss: the miser Mammon.

Mammon is this big ugly “be thou not afraid?” biblically accurate angel-type creature that looks like a wheel with an eyeball in the middle. My first few attempts to bring him down went poorly. He likes to erratically bounces about the arena, spits lines of fire at different angles, and tracks Rose’s position before brutally slamming down on her. I was having a devil of a time avoiding those attacks, as running away from one often put me in the danger zone of another. I just could not move fast enough to get away.

Frustrated, I took a break, popping on a speedrun of the game just to see the tips and tricks the professionals use to get through it. Turns out they parry, a lot. I don’t like the parry as a defense mechanism in Belmont’s Curse for the same reason I don’t like it in other nonâClair ObscurÂ games: It’s hard to do that shit on the fly. That difficulty is compounded because, as I’ve mentioned, Belmont’s Curse likes to throw everything at you, everywhere, all at once. The only reason I like parrying in Expedition 33 is because you’re just standing still waiting for the attack. Trying to figure out timings when 9 million projectiles are headed at your face is a fool’s errand, especially when the movement mechanics feel more like muscle memory to me than something I have to actively time.

But shit, I’d like to finish the game this century so I gave it a shot and it’s infuriating how well it worked. Instead of another gauntlet of failures, I beat Mammon within a handful of tries after picking the game back up. You know how in Zelda games, after you get a new item in a dungeon, its boss is often themed specifically around that item? That’s what this felt like, even though I’d picked up the parry four or so bosses previously. Belmont’s Curse gives you the freedom to find your own playstyle, but every so often it offers a test to check for understanding. I like that, it prevents things from getting too rote or stale. I don’t think I have the capacity to put the parry into my regular rotation, but next time I get stuck, I know to reach into my bag of tricks for something new.
